items.stem: Which term describes the following: “The extent to which a patient’s behaviour matches the medical advice they have been given”?
items.answer: Adherence
items.markingKey: Adherence: the extent to which a patient’s behaviour matches the medical advice they have been given. [1]

items.stem: Assertion (A): Forgetting to take a tablet is not rational non-adherence. Reason (R): Rational non-adherence involves a deliberate decision not to follow advice. Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
items.answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
items.markingKey: Forgetting is unintentional. [1]

items.stem: Explain the health belief model as an explanation of adherence.
items.answer: A person is more likely to adhere if they believe they are susceptible to an illness that is serious, that the treatment has benefits that outweigh the barriers (cost, side effects), and if there is a cue to action; self-efficacy may also be included.
items.markingKey: 1 mark susceptibility/severity; 1 mark benefits v barriers; 1 mark cues [3]

items.stem: Ravi, aged 55, from Mumbai, has high blood pressure but often skips tablets. Ravi feels well, finds the tablets cause tiredness and does not think the condition is serious. Suggest two ways the doctor could increase Ravi’s adherence.
items.answer: Explain the risks of untreated high blood pressure (increasing perceived severity) and change to a drug with fewer side effects (reducing barriers); use reminders as cues to action.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Elena, aged 55, from Manila, has high blood pressure but often skips tablets. Elena feels well, finds the tablets cause tiredness and does not think the condition is serious. (a) Identify the type of non-adherence shown by Elena. (b) Suggest two ways the doctor could increase Elena’s adherence.
items.answer: (a) Rational (intentional) non-adherence. (b) Explain the risks of untreated high blood pressure (increasing perceived severity) and change to a drug with fewer side effects (reducing barriers); use reminders as cues to action.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark [1] (b) 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Yusuf, aged 55, from Seoul, has high blood pressure but often skips tablets. Yusuf feels well, finds the tablets cause tiredness and does not think the condition is serious. (a) Use the health belief model to explain Yusuf’s non-adherence. (b) Suggest two ways the doctor could increase Yusuf’s adherence.
items.answer: (a) Low perceived severity (“not serious”) and susceptibility (feels well), and high perceived barriers (tiredness), so the benefits do not seem to outweigh the costs. (b) Explain the risks of untreated high blood pressure (increasing perceived severity) and change to a drug with fewer side effects (reducing barriers); use reminders as cues to action.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark severity/susceptibility; 1 mark barriers [2] (b) 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Evaluate the health belief model in terms of two strengths and two weaknesses. At least one of your evaluation points must be about usefulness.
items.answer: Strength (supporting evidence): Becker et al. found that mothers’ beliefs about susceptibility and severity were related to adherence measured by blood tests. Strength (usefulness): Interventions can target specific beliefs, for example increasing perceived severity or reducing barriers. Weakness (measurement): Components are measured by self-report and different studies measure them in different ways. Weakness (reductionism): It assumes rational decision-making and ignores emotions, habits and social pressure. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement about the overall value of the study.

items.stem: Which term describes the following: “Deliberately not following advice for reasons that make sense to the patient, such as side effects or cost”?
items.answer: Rational non-adherence
items.markingKey: Rational non-adherence: deliberately not following advice for reasons that make sense to the patient, such as side effects or cost. [1]

items.stem: A student writes: “Non-adherence to medication is very rare.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. Studies suggest a large proportion of patients (often estimated at around half) do not take medication exactly as prescribed.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: correct judgement; 1 mark: accurate explanation [2]

items.stem: Explain the difference between intentional and unintentional non-adherence.
items.answer: Intentional non-adherence is a deliberate decision (for example because of side effects); unintentional non-adherence happens without a decision, such as forgetting or misunderstanding instructions.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: A clinic in Madrid gave 6 children with asthma a fun spacer device with a whistle and spinning disc and 6 children a standard spacer. The number of days (out of 14) on which the inhaler was used as prescribed was recorded. Table: Days with correct use (out of 14) — Fun spacer: 11, 11, 11, 9, 13, 7. Standard spacer: 9, 8, 12, 7, 8, 7. The standard deviation for the fun spacer condition was 2.07 and for the standard spacer condition was 1.87. Explain what these values show.
items.answer: The fun spacer condition has the larger standard deviation, so its scores are more spread out around the mean; the other condition’s scores are more consistent.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the condition with the larger spread; 1 mark: explains that a larger SD means scores are more spread around the mean [2]

items.stem: Lina compared adherence (days out of 14 with correct inhaler use) for children using a fun spacer or a standard spacer. Table: Days with correct use (out of 14) — Fun spacer: 10, 12, 9, 10, 12, 10, 13. Standard spacer: 8, 8, 7, 5, 9, 6, 9. (a) Calculate the percentage of participants in the standard spacer condition who scored 9 or more. Show your working. (b) Describe one variable that should be controlled in this study and explain why.
items.answer: (a) 28.6% (b) The same inhaler medication and instructions.
items.markingKey: (a) 2 out of 7 participants scored 9 or more: 2 ÷ 7 × 100 = 28.6%. 1 mark working; 1 mark answer [2] (b) 1 mark: relevant control identified; 1 mark: explains how it would otherwise act as a confounding variable [2]

items.stem: Explain one strength and one weakness of pill counts as a measure of adherence.
items.answer: Strength: objective and cheap, not relying on memory or honesty. Weakness: removing pills does not prove they were taken correctly (pills may be thrown away or taken at the wrong time).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Explain why biological measures of adherence may be more valid than self-report.
items.answer: They show whether the drug is actually present in the body, so they are not affected by social desirability or poor memory, although levels also depend on metabolism.
items.markingKey: 1 mark presence in body; 1 mark not affected by bias [2]

items.stem: Lina, a patient in Bogotá, was prescribed 2 tablets a day for 21 days and given a bottle of 46 tablets. At the end of the period, a pill count found 23 tablets left. (a) Calculate the number of tablets that should have been taken. (b) Adherence of 80% or more is often treated as acceptable. State whether this patient meets the standard.

Mohammed, a patient in Jakarta, was prescribed 2 tablets a day for 14 days and given a bottle of 28 tablets. At the end of the period, a pill count found 10 tablets left. (a) Calculate the number of tablets that should have been taken. (b) Calculate the percentage adherence shown by the pill count. Give your answer to one decimal place.
items.markingKey: (a) 2 × 14 = 28 [1] (b) Taken = 28 − 10 = 18; 18 ÷ 28 × 100 = 64.3%. 1 mark tablets taken; 1 mark percentage [2]

items.stem: Elena, a patient in Jakarta, was prescribed 3 tablets a day for 14 days and given a bottle of 46 tablets. At the end of the period, a pill count found 21 tablets left. (a) Calculate the number of tablets that should have been taken. (b) Adherence of 80% or more is often treated as acceptable. State whether this patient meets the standard. (c) Explain why the pill count may overestimate adherence.
items.answer: (a) 42 (b) No (59.5%) (c) Tablets may have been removed but not taken (thrown away, lost or shared), or taken at the wrong times.
items.markingKey: (a) 3 × 14 = 42 [1] (b) 59.5% is below 80% [1] (c) 1 mark removal ≠ taking; 1 mark example [2]

items.stem: ‘Non-adherence is usually a rational decision.’ Discuss this view. In your answer, you may refer to individual differences, health belief model and usefulness.
items.answer: Arguments for: Patients may weigh side effects against benefits (rational non-adherence). The health belief model explains adherence through perceived costs and benefits. Arguments against: Much non-adherence is unintentional, such as forgetting. Complex regimens and poor communication cause non-adherence. Conclusion: a supported judgement weighing the evidence on both sides.

items.stem: A clinic in Auckland gave 6 children with asthma a fun spacer device with a whistle and spinning disc and 6 children a standard spacer. The number of days (out of 14) on which the inhaler was used as prescribed was recorded. Table: Days with correct use (out of 14) — Fun spacer: 10, 10, 11, 9, 10, 14. Standard spacer: 5, 8, 3, 8, 8, 8. Using the mean scores, state one conclusion that can be drawn from these results.
items.answer: The fun spacer condition had a higher mean (10.7) than the standard spacer condition (6.7), suggesting that a fun spacer improves children’s adherence to inhaler use.

items.stem: Lina, a patient in Cairo, was prescribed 2 tablets a day for 14 days and given a bottle of 34 tablets. At the end of the period, a pill count found 11 tablets left. (a) Calculate the number of tablets that should have been taken. (b) Explain why the pill count may overestimate adherence. (c) Suggest a more valid way of measuring this patient’s adherence and explain why.
items.answer: (a) 28 (b) Tablets may have been removed but not taken (thrown away, lost or shared), or taken at the wrong times. (c) A biological measure such as a blood test for the drug, or electronic monitoring of bottle openings, which does not rely on counting what is left.
items.markingKey: (a) 2 × 14 = 28 [1] (b) 1 mark removal ≠ taking; 1 mark example [2] (c) 1 mark method; 1 mark reason [2]

items.stem: Kwame compared adherence (days out of 14 with correct inhaler use) for children using a fun spacer or a standard spacer. Table: Days with correct use (out of 14) — Fun spacer: 10, 10, 9, 12, 11, 12. Standard spacer: 8, 8, 4, 11, 5, 10. (a) Name the experimental design used in this study and explain one weakness of using this design here. (b) The standard deviation for the fun spacer condition was 1.21 and for the standard spacer condition was 2.73. Explain what these values show. (c) To what extent do these results support the prediction that children using a fun spacer will use their inhaler as prescribed on more days than children using a standard spacer? Use the data in your answer. (d) Explain why a repeated measures design might have been used instead, and one problem this would cause.
items.answer: (a) Independent measures: different participants take part in each condition. Weakness: participant variables (individual differences between the two groups) may explain the difference in the DV instead of the IV. (b) The standard spacer condition has the larger standard deviation, so its scores are more spread out around the mean; the other condition’s scores are more consistent. (c) Mean for fun spacer = 10.7 and standard spacer = 7.7; the direction of the difference matches the prediction, but the scores in the two conditions overlap (ranges 3 and 7) and the sample is small (n = 6 per condition), so the results only partly support it; a statistical test would be needed to show the difference is significant. (d) Repeated measures removes participant variables because the same people do both conditions, but order effects (practice or fatigue) and demand characteristics become more likely; counterbalancing would be needed.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: correct design; 1 mark: weakness explained in context [2] (b) 1 mark: identifies the condition with the larger spread; 1 mark: explains that a larger SD means scores are more spread around the mean [2] (c) 1 mark: uses both means; 1 mark: judgement about direction; 1 mark: limitation such as overlap of scores, small sample or no statistical test [3] (d) 1 mark: advantage of the alternative design; 1 mark: problem it causes; 1 mark: applied to this study [3]

items.stem: Explain how operant conditioning can be used to improve adherence.
items.answer: Adherent behaviour is followed by a reward (praise, money, toys, tokens), so it is positively reinforced and more likely to be repeated; for example the Funhaler’s whistle rewards correct inhaler use.
items.markingKey: 1 mark reinforcement principle; 1 mark example [2]

items.stem: Describe the findings of Watt et al. (2003).
items.answer: Children aged about 1.5–6 years used the Funhaler (with a whistle and spinning disc) instead of a standard spacer; more parents reported medicating their child the previous day and using the correct technique with the Funhaler.
items.markingKey: 1 mark procedure; 1 mark findings [2]

items.answer: Adherence may fall when rewards stop, because the behaviour was maintained by the external reward.

items.stem: A clinic in Nairobi finds that many teenage patients with diabetes forget to check their blood sugar levels. (a) Suggest how reminders could be used. (b) Explain one problem with using rewards to improve adherence.
items.answer: (a) Send text-message or app alerts at times when checks are due, acting as cues to action. (b) Adherence may fall when rewards stop, because the behaviour was maintained by the external reward.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark reminder; 1 mark cue to action [2] (b) 1 mark extinction; 1 mark explained [2]

items.stem: Discuss the strengths and weaknesses of Watt et al.’s (2003) Funhaler study. Include at least one point about repeated measures.
items.answer: Strength (repeated measures): Each child used both the standard spacer and the Funhaler, so differences between children were controlled. Strength (usefulness): A cheap device could improve the management of asthma in young children. Weakness (sample size): The sample was small (about 30 children), so the results may not generalise. Weakness (self-report): Adherence was reported by parents, who may have exaggerated use of the new device. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement about the overall value of the study.

items.stem: Isla compared adherence (days out of 14 with correct inhaler use) for children using a fun spacer or a standard spacer. (b) Using the mean scores, state one conclusion that can be drawn from these results. (c) The participants were people selected from a full list of residents of Lima using a random number generator. Identify the sampling technique used and explain one weakness of it. (d) Suggest one improvement to this study and explain how it would improve the validity or reliability of the results. items.answer: (a) Fun spacer: 14; standard spacer: 7. (d) Randomly allocate participants to the conditions, to reduce the effect of participant variables. (e) Repeated measures removes participant variables because the same people do both conditions, but order effects (practice or fatigue) and demand characteristics become more likely; counterbalancing would be needed.
items.markingKey: (a) Fun spacer: 14 − 0 = 14; standard spacer: 12 − 5 = 7. 1 mark each [2] (b) 1 mark: conclusion about the effect of the IV on the DV; 1 mark: supported with the means [2] (c) 1 mark: sampling technique; 1 mark: weakness explained [2] (d) 1 mark: improvement; 1 mark: how to do it; 1 mark: effect on validity/reliability explained [3] (e) 1 mark: advantage of the alternative design; 1 mark: problem it causes; 1 mark: applied to this study [3]

items.stem: What is meant by ‘prompt’?
items.answer: A reminder, such as a letter, phone call or text message, to perform a health behaviour.
items.markingKey: Prompt: a reminder, such as a letter, phone call or text message, to perform a health behaviour. 1 mark for a partial definition; 2 marks for a full, accurate definition [2]

items.stem: With reference to Watt et al.’s (2003) Funhaler study, explain one weakness relating to sample size.
items.answer: The sample was small (about 30 children), so the results may not generalise.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies a relevant weakness linked to sample size; 1 mark: explained using detail from the study [2]

items.stem: Explain one strength of Watt et al.’s (2003) Funhaler study relating to repeated measures and one weakness relating to self-report.
items.answer: Strength (repeated measures): Each child used both the standard spacer and the Funhaler, so differences between children were controlled. Weakness (self-report): Adherence was reported by parents, who may have exaggerated use of the new device.
items.markingKey: 2 marks for each point: 1 mark identification, 1 mark explanation in the context of the study [4]

items.stem: A clinic in Lisbon finds that many teenage patients with diabetes forget to check their blood sugar levels. Explain one problem with using rewards to improve adherence.
items.answer: Adherence may fall when rewards stop, because the behaviour was maintained by the external reward.
items.markingKey: 1 mark extinction; 1 mark explained [2]

items.stem: A clinic in Santiago finds that many teenage patients with diabetes forget to check their blood sugar levels. (a) Suggest how reminders could be used. (b) Explain one problem with using rewards to improve adherence.
items.answer: (a) Send text-message or app alerts at times when checks are due, acting as cues to action. (b) Adherence may fall when rewards stop, because the behaviour was maintained by the external reward.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark reminder; 1 mark cue to action [2] (b) 1 mark extinction; 1 mark explained [2]

items.stem: Which term is defined as the following: “Triggers, such as symptoms or reminders, that prompt a person to take a health action”?
items.answer: Cues to action

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) A student writes: “Non-adherence to medication is very rare.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. (b) In a revision session, a student says: “Complex medication regimes can reduce adherence.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) Not correct. Studies suggest a large proportion of patients (often estimated at around half) do not take medication exactly as prescribed. (b) Correct. More doses and drugs make it harder to follow instructions.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: correct judgement; 1 mark: accurate explanation [2] (b) 1 mark: correct judgement; 1 mark: accurate explanation [2]

items.stem: The health belief model can be evaluated in terms of usefulness. Explain one strength of the study relating to this issue.
items.answer: Interventions can target specific beliefs, for example increasing perceived severity or reducing barriers.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies a relevant strength linked to usefulness; 1 mark: explained using detail from the study [2]

items.stem: Noah, aged 55, from Santiago, has high blood pressure but often skips tablets. Noah feels well, finds the tablets cause tiredness and does not think the condition is serious. Suggest two ways the doctor could increase Noah’s adherence.
items.answer: Explain the risks of untreated high blood pressure (increasing perceived severity) and change to a drug with fewer side effects (reducing barriers); use reminders as cues to action.

items.stem: Mateo, aged 55, from Auckland, has high blood pressure but often skips tablets. Mateo feels well, finds the tablets cause tiredness and does not think the condition is serious. (a) Use the health belief model to explain Mateo’s non-adherence. (b) Identify the type of non-adherence shown by Mateo.
items.answer: (a) Low perceived severity (“not serious”) and susceptibility (feels well), and high perceived barriers (tiredness), so the benefits do not seem to outweigh the costs. (b) Rational (intentional) non-adherence.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark severity/susceptibility; 1 mark barriers [2] (b) 1 mark [1]

items.stem: Assess the view that non-adherence is usually a rational decision.
items.answer: Arguments for: Patients may weigh side effects against benefits (rational non-adherence). The health belief model explains adherence through perceived costs and benefits. Arguments against: Much non-adherence is unintentional, such as forgetting. Complex regimens and poor communication cause non-adherence. Conclusion: a supported judgement weighing the evidence on both sides.

Top band: accurate, detailed psychological knowledge (named studies/theories) used to build a two-sided argument; evaluation includes issues such as validity, reliability, generalisability, ethics or usefulness; a justified conclusion. Middle band: relevant knowledge with some evaluation, but one side or the conclusion is underdeveloped. Lower band: limited, mostly descriptive answer with little evaluation.

items.stem: ‘Objective measures of adherence are better than subjective measures.’ Evaluate this statement, using evidence from psychology.
items.answer: Arguments for: Pill counts and electronic monitors (such as TrackCap) do not rely on honesty or memory. Biological measures (blood or urine tests) can show whether the drug has been taken. Arguments against: Removing pills from a bottle does not prove they were taken. Biological tests are invasive and costly. Self-report is cheap, quick and can reveal reasons for non-adherence. Conclusion: a supported judgement weighing the evidence on both sides.
items.markingKey: Levels of response. items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) A student writes: “Electronic monitoring proves that patients have taken their medication.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. items.answer: (a) Not correct. It shows when the container was opened, not that the dose was taken. (b) Correct. Methods can be compared to check agreement.

items.stem: Hana, a patient in Seoul, was prescribed 3 tablets a day for 14 days and given a bottle of 46 tablets. At the end of the period, a pill count found 24 tablets left. (a) Calculate the number of tablets that should have been taken. (b) Calculate the percentage adherence shown by the pill count. Give your answer to one decimal place.
items.markingKey: (a) 3 × 14 = 42 [1] (b) Taken = 46 − 24 = 22; 22 ÷ 42 × 100 = 52.4%. 1 mark tablets taken; 1 mark percentage [2]

items.stem: A researcher in Colombo is interested in why patients stop taking prescribed medication. Design an interview to test this. Your plan must include: the sampling technique, ethical issues, how the data will be analysed and one example question.
items.answer: Method: an interview. A structured or semi-structured interview with set questions asked in the same order; record and transcribe answers; train interviewers. Variables: topic: reasons for non-adherence; measure: rating scales and open answers. Sample: for example an opportunity or volunteer sample of about 30 people from the target population in Colombo, with reasons. Design/procedure: clear, replicable steps, with standardised instructions and random allocation or counterbalancing where relevant. Ethics: informed consent, right to withdraw, protection from harm, confidentiality and a full debrief. Data: quantitative scores summarised with means and a suitable graph; qualitative answers analysed into themes where collected.
items.markingKey: Levels of response. Top band: a detailed, accurate and replicable plan using the stated method; all required features are included and are appropriate to the aim; variables are operationalised; ethics are addressed. Middle band: a workable plan with most required features but some lack detail or are not justified. Lower band: a basic plan with few features or with errors in method.

items.stem: What is meant by ‘positive reinforcement for adherence’?
items.answer: Rewarding patients for following medical advice to increase future adherence.

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain how operant conditioning can be used to improve adherence. (b) Describe the findings of Watt et al. (2003).
items.answer: (a) Adherent behaviour is followed by a reward (praise, money, toys, tokens), so it is positively reinforced and more likely to be repeated; for example the Funhaler’s whistle rewards correct inhaler use. (b) Children aged about 1.5–6 years used the Funhaler (with a whistle and spinning disc) instead of a standard spacer; more parents reported medicating their child the previous day and using the correct technique with the Funhaler.
